column4: The source's dictionary form كذّابة is a dyed surface that looks embroidered without woven stitches; here rain strips soil from the rock, exposing the attractive cover as unsupported.
The section's root ر ء ي includes good appearance and public showing; this ayah says their bodies please the viewer, then compares them to propped-up logs, separating display from what sustains it.

The section sets the root ك ذ ب against truth and says deeds expose a false surface; this ayah says turning one's face is not righteousness, then names giving, prayer and patience as the deeds of those who are truthful (صَدَقُوا).

The section's root ر ء ي opens with “Have you seen?” and its running image includes a movement that fails to continue; this ayah asks about the one who turned away (تَوَلَّىٰ), introducing the concrete withdrawal in its next verse.

The source's dictionary idiom for the camel's milk is that it was expected to last but stopped; this adjacent ayah says he gave a little, then stopped (أَكْدَىٰ), making the failed continuation explicit.
Against the source's prayer performed only while watched, this ayah describes people who remain constant (دَائِمُونَ) in prayer; the continuity is the opposite of stopping when the audience leaves.
The section contrasts a showy prayer that is abandoned with sustained prayer; this ayah says they guard (يُحَافِظُونَ) their prayers, naming the continuation the image lacks.
The section stresses being “away from” prayer (عن) while appearing to pray; this ayah places humility “in” prayer (فِي صَلَاتِهِمْ), a direct boundary between the two stances.

The section says the painted exterior must answer to inward intention; this ayah joins prayer and almsgiving to making religion sincere for God (مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ), the opposite of an audience-facing surface.
This ayah directly names failure to honor the orphan (لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ), the action by which the section says the denier of dīn is exposed.
This ayah says they do not urge feeding the poor (وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ), matching the section's concrete measure of a life whose claim of religion is not carried into action.
The command to do good to orphans and the needy gives the positive action against the section's orphan-pushing and failure to encourage food for the poor.
This ayah joins miserliness to urging others to be miserly and concealing God's bounty; that is a specific opposite of the section's expected giving and its exposed inner state.
The source's root ر ء ي includes public showing; this ayah describes spending “to be seen by people” (رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ) while lacking belief in God and the Last Day, joining display to denied dīn.
This ayah combines rising lazily for prayer with “showing people” (يُرَاءُونَ النَّاسَ) and little remembrance; it makes the section's prayer-away and public surface explicit.
This ayah says their prayer is approached lazily and their spending reluctantly; those half-present acts give a direct counterpart to the section's interrupted prayer and failed giving.
The source's idioms describe a beginning that promises continuation but does not hold; this adjacent ayah introduces a pledge to give charity if bounty comes, whose reversal follows.
After the pledge in 9:75, this ayah says that when bounty came they became miserly and turned away; the beginning does not hold through to the promised act.

The source explicitly says ك ذ ب can describe conduct, not only speech; this ayah links breaking their promise to hypocrisy and says they used to lie (يَكْذِبُونَ), naming both the failed deed and falsehood.
The section says a life can lie through what it does; this ayah asks why people say what they do not do, stating that mismatch directly.
This adjacent ayah calls it greatly hateful to say what one does not do; it supplies the judgment on the speech-and-action split named in 61:2.

The section's root ك ذ ب names a failed continuation; this ayah calls those who were true to their covenant with God (صَدَقُوا مَا عَاهَدُوا) and says some fulfilled it while others await without changing.

The section's painted cloth seems to carry woven content without having it; this ayah compares those entrusted with scripture but not carrying it out to a donkey carrying books, an unusually exact image of outside possession without inward realization.

This ayah describes spending without following it with reminders or injury, showing how the act must continue in conduct after the visible gift; that is the section's test of whether the apparent good is real.
A kind word and pardon are called better than charity followed by injury; this gives a precise boundary for the section's claim that visible giving can be contradicted by what follows.
After the rock whose soil washes away in 2:264, this adjacent parable shows a garden rooted on high ground yielding fruit; it contrasts a surface coating with growth that has a real root.
The command not to choose inferior things for charity, which one would accept only with closed eyes, directly tests whether a gift's apparent value matches its substance.
This ayah says charity given openly or kept hidden is known to God and that hidden giving is better; it distinguishes an audience-facing display from the inner intention emphasized in the section.
This ayah describes spending by night and day, secretly and openly, with reward from God; sustained giving whose worth is not confined to spectators reverses the section's show.

The source's dictionary form دَانَ يَدينُ leaves the oath-taker to his intention; this ayah likewise distinguishes unintentional oaths from what hearts have earned, locating judgment beneath the words.

The source's dictionary form about an oath-taker turns on intention; this ayah distinguishes careless oaths from deliberate ones (عَقَّدتُّمُ الْأَيْمَانَ), giving the same word-versus-intent boundary in its own context.

The section's deceptive cloth only looks woven; this ayah warns against a woman who unspins her yarn after making it strong (نَقَضَتْ غَزْلَهَا), a contrary textile image of an actual construction undone after a pledge.
This adjacent passage begins by describing people who fulfill vows and fear a difficult day; it gives a sustained response to the source's promise that a beginning can fail to continue.
The ayah describes feeding the orphan, poor person and captive, directly reversing the section's orphan-pushing and failure to urge food for the poor.
They explain that they feed only for God's sake and seek neither reward nor thanks (لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ); the declared inward motive is the opposite of performing for an audience.
This ayah specifies a known right in wealth for the asker and deprived person, placing material provision immediately after the constant prayer in 70:23.
This adjacent ayah names the asker and deprived person as the holders of that right, making the section's concern with feeding and withholding concrete.
In their own account of why they are in Saqar, they say they were not among those who prayed; it directly links denied dīn to prayer absent from life.
The next answer says they did not feed the poor; it supplies the same concrete failure to give that the section uses to expose the denier.
They say they used to deny the Day of Recompense (يَوْمِ الدِّينِ); this directly names the denial whose practical signs the section traces through the orphan, poor and prayer.
The opening woe for those who give short measure introduces people whose outward exchange hides a deliberate shortfall, a concrete lie in action as the source's root ك ذ ب allows.
This adjacent ayah says they take full measure from others, establishing the imbalance that makes their own short measure a false outward dealing.
This adjacent ayah says that when they measure or weigh for others they give less; the action itself falls short of what the exchange appears to promise.
The passage asks whether these short-measurers think they will be raised; it completes the connection between the deceptive act and the judgment denied in the section.
This next ayah names the great Day on which they will be raised, completing the judgment scene introduced after the short measure.
It says mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds; the specific dishonest measure is thus answerable to the judgment the section hears within دِين.
After the short-measure passage, this ayah announces woe for deniers (لِلْمُكَذِّبِينَ); it names the falsehood behind the conduct rather than leaving it as a mere commercial mistake.
The following ayah specifies that these deniers reject the Day of Recompense; this joins the conduct in 83:1–3 to the denied dīn in the source.
This ayah says their earnings have covered their hearts; that is a specific inward result of deeds covering what is beneath, completing the section's surface-and-interior image.
The speaker boasts, “I have squandered abundant wealth” (أَهْلَكْتُ مَالًا لُّبَدًا); this gives a concrete public claim of spending whose real measure is tested by what follows.
The next ayah asks whether he thinks no one sees him (أَن لَّمْ يَرَهُ أَحَدٌ); it puts the source's unseen intention and public appearance under God's gaze.
After the boast of wealth, this ayah asks about the steep path; the following verses define what real, difficult giving entails, rather than treating a spending claim as enough.
The first act on the steep path is freeing a person from bondage, a costly deed that contrasts with a merely impressive surface or claim.
The next act is feeding during a day of hunger, directly opposing the section's failure to urge food for the poor.
This ayah specifies feeding an orphan who is a relative (يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ), the direct opposite of pushing the orphan away.
This ayah specifies feeding a needy person in severe poverty (مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ), making the section's withheld provision concrete.
Belief is paired with urging one another to patience and compassion; this adds an enduring communal response to the feeding acts, unlike the section's halted care.
The next ayah identifies those who do these things as the companions of the right; their deeds, rather than a display, establish their standing.
The garden owners go off whispering together before the harvest; their concealed plan begins the concrete refusal to share provision that the section marks as evidence.
Their whisper is made explicit: they resolve that no poor person will enter the garden; this directly stages failure to encourage or provide food.
They leave early, confident and determined to keep the harvest; this shows a sustained, purposeful action in the very direction opposite to giving.
The command not to oppress or repel the orphan (فَلَا تَقْهَرْ) directly reverses the section's image of pushing the orphan away.
The next command not to rebuke the one who asks (فَلَا تَنْهَرْ) gives a concrete counterpart to the section's treatment of the vulnerable petitioner.
This ayah says hypocritical men and women close their hands, command evil and forbid good; its withheld hand gives the section's denial a specific material action.
The same passage recalls Abraham, “the one who fulfilled” (وَفَّىٰ); this continuing example supplies the opposite of the section's start that does not carry through.
The passage says a human being has only what he strives for; it gives the interrupted giving in 53:34 its measure in actual effort.
The following ayah says that his striving will be seen; it connects the source's “Have you seen?” framing to deeds that are exposed and assessed.
The command to guard the prayers (حَافِظُوا عَلَى الصَّلَوَاتِ) is a direct opposite to being away from prayer or stopping when unobserved.
After describing humility in prayer in 23:2, this ayah says the believers guard their prayers; it adds continued care to the inward presence contrasted with the section's inattention.
This ayah says prayer restrains indecency and wrongdoing; it connects the section's visible prayer movements to the conduct that should follow from prayer.

The section's painted surface looks as if it contains a woven inner pattern; these people say they believe in God and the Last Day while the ayah says they are not believers, a specific claim-versus-reality split.
This next ayah says they think they deceive God and believers but deceive only themselves; it makes the apparent surface and hidden reality in 2:8 explicit.
The next ayah names disease in their hearts and says they lie (يَكْذِبُونَ); it connects inner condition to the section's root for a lie expressed in one's state.
They tell believers they believe, then privately say they were only mocking; this is a specific outward claim and concealed stance like the section's false surface.
The question “Do you command righteousness and forget yourselves?” names speech whose own conduct fails it, the same action-level falsehood developed from the source's root ك ذ ب.
The command not to mix truth with falsehood or conceal truth (لَا تَلْبِسُوا الْحَقَّ بِالْبَاطِلِ) gives a verbal counterpart to the source's surface that appears to contain a pattern it does not.
This repeated command asks why truth is mixed with falsehood and knowingly concealed; it independently restates the hidden-under-cover relation of the painted cloth.
The ayah says righteousness is not attained until one spends what one loves; the real cost of a gift tests the inner commitment behind its visible appearance.
Those who love praise for what they did not do are named alongside rejoicing in what they did; the gap between public credit and actual deed directly fits the section's false surface.

This ayah pairs prayer and spending, done privately and publicly, with seeking God's face and repelling evil with good; the explicit intention and continuing response clarify what a merely displayed act lacks.

The ayah describes reciting scripture, establishing prayer and spending secretly and openly while hoping for a trade that will not fail; its sustained, inwardly directed acts reverse the source's short-lived display.
The needy are restrained from asking and appear self-sufficient, yet their need can be recognized by their marks; this is a specific reversal in which outward appearance hides the real condition.

These are people whose effort is lost in worldly life while they think they are doing well; the explicit misreading of their own performance parallels a life whose surface looks right but does not hold.
Wealth and children are called the adornment of worldly life, while lasting good deeds are better; this gives the source's painted adornment a specific contrast with what truly remains.

The ayah compares worldly life to growth that first pleases and adorns the earth, then yellows and breaks; its visible beauty and cessation parallel the source's appearance and interrupted continuation.

The earth's growth first adorns itself, then is cut down as though it had not flourished; the specific change from attractive surface to absence echoes the source's false appearance and stopped motion.
The source's dictionary sense of د ي ن leaves the oath-taker to intent; this ayah says God knows what people spend and vow, connecting intention to accountable acts.
This ayah says people take their oaths as a shield and turn others from God's way; a protective-looking exterior concealing contrary intent fits the section's painted covering.
On the Day all are raised, the hypocrites swear to God as they swear to people and think they stand on something; the repeated false oath makes the section's word-versus-intention theme specific.

The ayah describes people going out boastfully and showing off to others (رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ); this is a concrete public display corresponding to the source's root ر ء ي and its audience-facing appearance.
The hypocrites are described as wavering between two sides (مُّذَبْذَبِينَ); this names an unstable, unfinished stance, a specific boundary against the section's faithful continuation.
This ayah says the person neither believed nor prayed; it is a direct opposite to 107's outward prayer that does not inhabit the prayer.
The next ayah says he denied and turned away; beside 75:31 it supplies the explicit denial that the section depicts through deeds.
